cards.title: Select columns
cards.question: How do you return only employee_name and salary from the employees table?
cards.answer: Use SELECT employee_name, salary FROM employees; SELECT names the output columns, and FROM identifies the source table.

definition.text: SELECT reads a result from data. Name the columns you need after SELECT and the source table after FROM.

concept.text: Imagine choosing columns from a spreadsheet. The stored table stays the same. SELECT * requests every column; naming columns makes the intended output clearer.

examples.text: Result: only the two requested columns. ORDER BY fixes the displayed row order.

syntax.text: End the statement with a semicolon. Without ORDER BY, do not rely on a particular row order.

cards.title: Distinct results
cards.question: A department appears on several employee rows. How can you return each department just once?
cards.answer: Use SELECT DISTINCT department FROM employees; DISTINCT removes duplicate rows from the query result, without deleting stored employee records.

definition.text: DISTINCT keeps one copy of each distinct result row.

concept.text: With several selected columns, the entire combination determines duplication. DISTINCT department, employee_name can still produce several rows for one department.

examples.text: Result: Sales appears once, although two employees belong to it.

syntax.text: Place DISTINCT immediately after SELECT. It changes the result, not the table.

cards.title: Filter with WHERE
cards.question: How do you return employees whose salary is at least 60000?
cards.answer: Add WHERE salary >= 60000. A row is included only when this condition is true; 60000 itself is included.

definition.text: WHERE keeps rows that satisfy a condition before the result is returned.

concept.text: Compare each row's salary with the threshold. >= means greater than or equal to; > would exclude a salary of exactly 60000.

examples.code:
SELECT employee_name, salary
FROM employees
WHERE salary >= 60000
ORDER BY employee_id;

examples.text: Result: Ben qualifies at the boundary; Chen qualifies above it.

syntax.text: Write WHERE after FROM. Combine conditions with AND or OR when you need more than one test.

cards.title: Find missing values
cards.question: Which condition finds employees with no department value: department = NULL or department IS NULL?
cards.answer: Use department IS NULL. NULL represents a missing value; an ordinary equality comparison with NULL does not evaluate to true.

definition.text: IS NULL tests whether a value is missing. IS NOT NULL tests whether it is present.

concept.text: NULL is not the number zero or the text 'NULL'. A comparison such as department = NULL has an unknown result, and WHERE keeps only true conditions.

examples.text: Input: employees. NULL in this table means a missing database value, not a word stored as text.

examples.code:
SELECT employee_name
FROM employees
WHERE department IS NULL
ORDER BY employee_id;

examples.text: Result: Ben is the only employee with no department value.

syntax.text: To find recorded departments instead, change IS NULL to IS NOT NULL.

cards.title: Inner Join
cards.question: Which join lists customers together with their matching orders, excluding customers who have no orders?
cards.answer: Use INNER JOIN with a matching condition such as c.customer_id = o.customer_id. Each matching pair becomes a result row; customers with no match are omitted.

diagram.alt: Only the overlap is shaded: keep matches between the two tables. This is a membership guide; the result can contain several rows per customer.

definition.text: An inner join returns pairs of rows that satisfy its join condition.

concept.text: Match each customer's ID to the customer ID on an order. A customer with two orders appears twice; a customer with no orders does not appear.

examples.code:
SELECT c.customer_name, o.order_id
FROM customers c
INNER JOIN orders o
  ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
ORDER BY c.customer_id, o.order_id;

examples.text: Result: two orders give Asha two rows. Ben has no match.

syntax.code:
SELECT c.customer_name, o.order_id
FROM customers c
INNER JOIN orders o
  ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id;

syntax.text: c and o are table aliases. Prefix shared column names with an alias to show which table supplies them.

cards.title: Left Join
cards.question: How can you list every customer and any matching orders, including customers with no orders?
cards.answer: Put customers on the left of a LEFT JOIN. Matching orders are returned; a customer without a match still gets a row, with NULLs for the order columns.

diagram.alt: The whole left circle, including the overlap, is shaded: preserve every left-table row and add matching right-table data. Several matches can produce several result rows.

definition.text: A left join preserves all rows from the left table. It adds matching right-table values, or NULLs when there is no match.

concept.text: Keep the customer list intact. Two matching orders still produce two rows for one customer. A later WHERE condition on the right table can remove unmatched rows, so choose filter placement carefully.

examples.code:
SELECT c.customer_name, o.order_id
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o
  ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
ORDER BY c.customer_id, o.order_id;

examples.text: Result: Ben remains, with a missing order value. NULL is not the text 'NULL' stored in the table.

syntax.code:
SELECT c.customer_name, o.order_id
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o
  ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id;

syntax.text: The table before LEFT JOIN is the preserved side. LEFT OUTER JOIN is another spelling of this join.
